title: How to think about teens' plummeting test scores
author: Jenny Anderson
summary: Jenny Anderson, co-author of The Disengaged Teen, responds to the latest PISA decline by granting the technology case and then arguing it is incomplete. She accepts that smartphones displaced sleep, reading and in-person connection, that too much ed-tech landed in classrooms without evidence, and that screens deserve the comeuppance they are getting. Her addition is the piece nobody is discussing: the retreat from asking children to do rigorous work. She invokes the Learning Pit and productive struggle, and observes that England, with its exam-heavy system and limited grade inflation, outperformed peers while her own children plodded through poetry and endless maths revision. She is careful not to romanticize it, noting the UK system's rote content crowds out student agency. The prescriptions are concrete and include grade inflation as a harm, substitution rather than suppression of screens, demanding ed-tech efficacy evidence of the kind New York City is now collecting, caution about blanket bans that push devices underground, and family engagement, which she calls the most underreported idea in learning. Her closing prediction is that those who blame tech alone will be disappointed when the tech goes away and scores do not move.
points: Anderson's structural move is to concede the entire screens argument and then argue it cannot carry the whole explanation.
She names grade inflation as an active harm, arguing easy As keep parents in the dark about where their children's learning gaps actually are.
Her comparative evidence is personal and hedged, crediting England's exam-heavy system for rigor while faulting it for crowding out agency.
On bans she warns that what schools prohibit tends to migrate into homes and underground, given that children are awake outside school roughly five thousand hours a year.
She cites PISA data that the share of hasty readers nearly doubled between 2018 and 2025, with the steepest declines among wealthy students.
quotes: People have been quick to land on technology as the most convincing culprit. Although PISA doesn’t show direct cause and effect, Andreas Schleicher, the OECD guy behind all the data, said this: “We cannot say for sure, but declining levels of reading for enjoyment and the shift towards digital reading – skimming social media feeds and rapidly processing information – may be compromising the ability of students to engage with complex texts and data.
Screens deserve the comeuppance they are getting. I wish Big Tech companies didn’t intentionally design products to addict our kids: Endless scroll, like buttons, forever comparison platforms.

But there’s a piece to this which isn’t being discussed: The importance of asking kids to do rigorous work. Setting high expectations and letting kids struggle to meet them. We talk at length in our book about the ‘Learning Pit,’ and how true learning comes from productive struggle. I even wrote about it in the NYT.

As parents and as educators, we have been loath to have kids do the sometimes-boring, often uncomfortable and definitely hard work of knowledge accumulation and content mastery. The UK, with its exam-heavy system and limited grade inflation, has not shied away from this (and did far better on PISA than most of its peers). British kids take pen-and-paper exams so they practice with analog tests and writing essays.

There is too much rote learning in the UK system, and so much content that we seriously crowd out any chance of developing Explorer Mode and student agency. The content feels meaningless to too many kids who give up on education because it all seems irrelevant.
Encourage kids to read books. PISA showed the share of "hasty readers" – students who rushed through texts and gave quick but incorrect answers – almost doubled between 2018 and 2025.

Parents can wait til 14 for phones and 16 for social media (brilliant) and Silicon Valley can be ordered to design safety products (it’s about damn time). I am all for banning phones in schools and only using products that have an evidence base behind them. I cheer the parents advocating for their kids’ to have less tech-saturated schools.

It’s also how kids fill any time they reclaim from screens that will make the difference: What curriculum? What books? What struggle? What rigor? What activities? What relationships? Importantly: In what environments?
